east.label: China–Russia-aligned
east.what: China, Russia and the states that lean on them for money, weapons or cover at the UN.

other.label: Unaligned
other.what: No strong lean either way, or not enough weight for the lean to matter to the board.

swing.label: Swing
swing.what: Large countries that deliberately trade with both sides and sign up with neither. Most of the world's growth is here.

west.label: US-led
west.what: The US alliance system: NATO, the EU, and America's treaty allies in Asia and the Pacific.

conflictStatus.ceasefire: Fighting paused under a ceasefire that could break.
conflictStatus.standoff: Armed confrontation without a war — yet.

conflicts.headline: The April ceasefire collapsed in July. The US blockade holds, Hormuz runs at about half its normal flow, and envoys are talking in New York.
conflicts.name: Iran war
conflicts.nameTh: สงครามอิหร่าน
conflicts.now: A Pakistan-brokered ceasefire on 8 April led to talks in Islamabad, which failed. The US has blockaded Iranian ports since 13 April. The ceasefire collapsed in early July when Iran attacked ships in Hormuz. Escorted convoys have brought the strait back to about half its normal flow. US and Iranian envoys met in New York on 22 September.
conflicts.stakes: Brent has spent most of the war close to or above $100, in what the IEA calls the largest oil supply disruption in history. Gulf LNG (Qatar) is cut too, so gas and power prices rise with oil.
conflicts.thailand: Thailand imports most of its crude from the Gulf and part of its LNG from Qatar. This war is the main driver of Thai fuel, electricity and inflation this year.
conflicts.watch: The New York talks, any reopening of Hormuz, attacks on Gulf oil infrastructure, and the US elections on 3 November, after which Trump has said the war will end.
conflicts.what: US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February 2026, aimed at Iran's nuclear programme and at regime change. The opening salvo killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones at US bases across the Gulf and closed the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia and the UAE later struck Iran too; Russia gave Iran intelligence and China sent dual-use parts.

conflicts.headline: The Houthis took Yemen's whole Red Sea coast in September, threatening the Saudi oil route around Hormuz.
conflicts.name: Red Sea and the Houthis
conflicts.nameTh: ทะเลแดงและกลุ่มฮูตี
conflicts.now: In September 2026 the Houthis took Yemen's whole Red Sea coast and Mayun island at the mouth of the strait. That threatens the route Saudi Arabia uses to export oil around Hormuz. Drones launched from Iraq also damaged the Saudi East–West pipeline, which will be mostly out of service for weeks; no Saudi crude has left Yanbu since 11 September.

sides.label: Saudi Arabia, the US and shipping

conflicts.stakes: With Hormuz throttled, the Red Sea is the Gulf's other exit. Losing both at once would cut off most Gulf oil exports. Shipping and insurance costs rise with every attack.
conflicts.thailand: Thai cargo to Europe goes through the Red Sea and Suez, or the long way around Africa, adding cost and weeks. It also threatens the Saudi oil Thailand buys.
conflicts.watch: Attacks on tankers leaving Yanbu, repairs to the Saudi pipeline, and any US or Saudi move to retake the coast.
conflicts.what: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have attacked ships near the Bab el-Mandeb strait since late 2023. Most container lines now sail around Africa instead of through Suez.

conflicts.headline: No ceasefire. Russia rejected an energy truce; three-way talks may resume in October.
conflicts.name: Russia–Ukraine war
conflicts.nameTh: สงครามรัสเซีย–ยูเครน
conflicts.now: No ceasefire. US envoys met Putin on 5 September and Zelenskyy on 6 September. Russia rejected an energy or air truce and demands the rest of Donbas. Both sides strike each other's energy systems ahead of winter, and three-way talks may resume in October.
conflicts.stakes: Gas, wheat and fertiliser prices, Europe's defence spending, and how much Russian oil still reaches India and China. Russia is also the big winner from high oil prices during the Iran war.
conflicts.thailand: Reaches Thailand through fuel, fertiliser and wheat prices, and through Russian tourists, one of Thailand's largest groups of visitors.
conflicts.watch: October talks, winter strikes on the power grids, and US tariffs on buyers of Russian oil.
conflicts.what: Russia's full-scale invasion from February 2022, after it seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in 2014. North Korea supplies Russia with shells and sent troops; Europe now pays for most of the US weapons that reach Ukraine.

conflicts.headline: Coast-guard patrols and blockade drills, with a US arms package on the table at this week's Trump–Xi summit.
conflicts.name: Taiwan Strait
conflicts.nameTh: ช่องแคบไต้หวัน
conflicts.now: China's coast guard now patrols east of the island and the military rehearses blockades. A pending US arms package is a bargaining chip at this week's Trump–Xi summit in Washington.
conflicts.stakes: TSMC makes about 90% of the most advanced chips. Markets fear a blockade more than an invasion: it would stop the AI supply chain within weeks, and Taiwan holds only days to weeks of energy.
conflicts.thailand: A shock to the electronics chain Thailand is part of, and to the Taiwanese firms now building servers and circuit boards in Thailand.
conflicts.watch: What the summit says about Taiwan and the arms package, and Chinese military drills after it.
conflicts.what: Beijing claims Taiwan and has not ruled out force. US law commits Washington to arm Taiwan, not to fight for it. In November 2025 Japan's prime minister said an attack on Taiwan could draw Japan in, and China has squeezed Japan economically ever since.

conflicts.headline: Three China–Philippines clashes in one week in July, and China is fencing off Scarborough Shoal.
conflicts.name: South China Sea
conflicts.nameTh: ทะเลจีนใต้
conflicts.now: Chinese and Philippine vessels clashed three times in one week in July 2026 at Scarborough and Second Thomas shoals, with water cannon. China has put barriers and a floating structure at Scarborough, and the US, Japan and the Philippines answered with joint drills.
conflicts.stakes: About a third of world shipping crosses it. A clash with a US treaty ally could trigger the alliance.
conflicts.thailand: Most of Thailand's trade with China, Japan and Korea sails through it. Thailand has no claim of its own.
conflicts.watch: Any Chinese construction at Scarborough, and resupply runs to Second Thomas Shoal.
conflicts.what: China claims most of the sea inside its 'nine-dash line', which an international tribunal rejected in 2016. The Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia claim parts of it. China took control of Scarborough Shoal from the Philippines in 2012.

conflicts.headline: The ceasefire holds, but crossings stay closed and Thailand has cancelled the maritime MOU.
conflicts.name: Thailand–Cambodia border
conflicts.nameTh: ชายแดนไทย–กัมพูชา
conflicts.now: The ceasefire holds, but relations are cold. Border crossings stay closed, Thailand has cancelled the 2001 MOU 44 on overlapping maritime claims, and Cambodia says Thai troops hold its territory. Both governments say they want practical confidence-building.
conflicts.stakes: Small for world markets. Cambodia is China's closest partner in ASEAN, so the border is also a quiet test of the region's balance.
conflicts.thailand: Home. Border trade, Cambodian workers in Thailand, and the overlapping maritime area in the Gulf of Thailand, which holds gas.
conflicts.watch: Crossings reopening, and whether talks on the maritime area start again.
conflicts.what: A long dispute over border temples turned into five days of fighting in July 2025, with artillery, rockets and Thai air strikes, and flared again in December 2025. Ceasefires were brokered with US involvement.

conflicts.headline: A ceasefire on paper since 16 April, with Israeli strikes continuing.
conflicts.name: Israel–Hezbollah (Lebanon)
conflicts.nameTh: อิสราเอล–ฮิซบอลเลาะห์
conflicts.now: A US-brokered ceasefire has held on paper since 16 April, but Israel keeps striking what it calls Hezbollah breaches. More than 4,000 people have been killed in Lebanon and over a million displaced.
conflicts.stakes: One of the Iran war's fronts. It matters to markets mainly as part of that war.
conflicts.thailand: Little direct link, beyond Thai workers in northern Israel.
conflicts.watch: Whether it reignites if the Iran war escalates.
conflicts.what: Hezbollah attacked Israel on 2 March 2026 after the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader, and Israel invaded southern Lebanon.

conflicts.headline: Quiet since the May 2025 war, with back-channel meetings but no formal talks.
conflicts.name: India–Pakistan (Kashmir)
conflicts.nameTh: อินเดีย–ปากีสถาน
conflicts.now: The ceasefire holds and back-channel meetings continue, but there is no formal dialogue. Pakistan's standing in Washington rose after it brokered the April 2026 US–Iran ceasefire, while India's ties with the US are strained over trade.
conflicts.stakes: Two nuclear powers, and a new attack could restart fighting within days. It weighs on Indian markets and emerging-market sentiment.
conflicts.thailand: Little direct link. India and Pakistan are both Thailand's rivals in rice exports.
conflicts.what: Both claim Kashmir and both have nuclear weapons. After a militant attack at Pahalgam in April 2025, India struck Pakistan and the two fought for four days in May 2025 before a ceasefire.

conflicts.headline: The ceasefire is in phase two, but Israel holds two-thirds of the strip and strikes continue.
conflicts.name: Gaza
conflicts.now: A US-backed ceasefire since 10 October 2025 moved to phase two in January 2026. Hamas's civil administration resigned in July and a disarmament deal followed, but Israel refuses to withdraw until Hamas disarms and holds about two-thirds of the strip. Strikes continue: over 1,300 killed since the ceasefire.
conflicts.stakes: Small direct market impact now. It shapes Israel's ties with the Gulf and its isolation abroad.
conflicts.thailand: Tens of thousands of Thai farm workers in Israel; Thais were among those killed and taken hostage in 2023.
conflicts.watch: Disarmament, Israeli withdrawal, and reconstruction money.
conflicts.what: Hamas's attack on 7 October 2023 and Israel's war in Gaza that followed. Thais were among the victims and hostages.

conflicts.headline: The RSF besieges El-Obeid while the army holds Khartoum and the east. Nearly 12 million displaced.
conflicts.name: Sudan civil war
conflicts.nameTh: สงครามกลางเมืองซูดาน
conflicts.now: The army holds Khartoum and the east; the RSF holds Darfur after taking El Fasher in October 2025, and is besieging El-Obeid. Several RSF commanders defected in August. Nearly 12 million people are displaced, and famine is confirmed in El Fasher and Kadugli.
conflicts.stakes: The world's largest humanitarian crisis. Its market impact is small: gold smuggling, and security on the Red Sea around Port Sudan.
conflicts.watch: El-Obeid, and US pressure on the outside backers.
conflicts.what: A power struggle between the army and the RSF paramilitary became a civil war in April 2023. The UAE is widely accused of arming the RSF, which it denies; Egypt and Turkey back the army. UN investigators say foreign support is what keeps it going.

conflicts.headline: Seoul and Washington want talks; Kim refuses and tests an upgraded hypersonic missile.
conflicts.name: Korean Peninsula
conflicts.nameTh: คาบสมุทรเกาหลี
conflicts.now: At the UN on 23 September, President Lee pressed for US–North Korea talks. Kim rejects any phased deal and says he will never talk to Seoul. The North tested an upgraded hypersonic missile this month.
conflicts.stakes: Korean chipmakers and Japanese markets carry the risk. North Korean hackers are also the largest thieves of crypto.
conflicts.watch: Missile tests, and whether Trump meets Kim.
conflicts.what: The 1953 armistice never became a peace treaty. North Korea has nuclear weapons, declared the South a 'hostile state' in 2023, and signed a defence pact with Russia in 2024.

conflicts.headline: Fighting again: Pakistan struck ten sites in Afghanistan on 24 September after drone attacks on its border posts.
conflicts.name: Pakistan–Afghanistan
conflicts.nameTh: ปากีสถาน–อัฟกานิสถาน
conflicts.now: A mediated ceasefire followed within weeks but never settled the TTP question, and low-level fighting went on. On 24 September 2026 Pakistan hit ten sites inside Afghanistan after drone attacks on its border posts.
conflicts.stakes: Small for markets. It stretches Pakistan's army and budget.
conflicts.what: Pakistan accuses the Taliban government of sheltering the Pakistani Taliban (TTP). Clashes began in October 2025. After an Afghan cross-border offensive on 26 February 2026, Pakistan declared 'open war' and bombed Kabul and Kandahar.

conflicts.headline: Stalemate. The junta leader became president after an election held only in army-held areas.
conflicts.name: Myanmar civil war
conflicts.nameTh: สงครามกลางเมืองเมียนมา
conflicts.now: A stalemate: resistance groups and ethnic armies hold more territory than the junta. After an election held only in army-held areas, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing became president in April 2026.
conflicts.stakes: Small for world markets. China brokers deals with the ethnic armies along its border to protect its pipelines.
conflicts.thailand: On Thailand's western border: refugees, scam compounds, drugs, and the Myanmar gas fields that supply part of Thailand's power.
conflicts.watch: China-brokered deals in the north, and fighting near the Thai border.
conflicts.what: The army's coup in February 2021 set off a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people.

conflicts.headline: Fighting goes on despite two peace deals; a roadmap for talks was agreed in August.
conflicts.name: Eastern Congo (M23)
conflicts.nameTh: คองโกตะวันออก
conflicts.now: A US-brokered Congo–Rwanda deal (2025) and a Doha framework with M23 (November 2025) have not stopped the fighting. A roadmap for talks was agreed in August 2026.
conflicts.stakes: The region holds much of the world's cobalt, tantalum and tin, which go into every phone and battery. Access to them was part of the US deal.
conflicts.thailand: No direct link, beyond battery-metal prices.
conflicts.watch: Whether talks under the August roadmap begin.
conflicts.what: M23 rebels took the cities of Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. The UN and Western governments say Rwanda backs them with troops and weapons; Rwanda denies it.

conflicts.headline: Jihadists are on the offensive in Mali, and Russia's Africa Corps has pulled back to guard Bamako.
conflicts.name: Sahel insurgency (Mali)
conflicts.now: In 2026 JNIM and Tuareg rebels went on the offensive in Mali. The defence minister was killed near Bamako, and Russia's Africa Corps withdrew from Kidal and now escorts convoys into the capital.

sides.label: Military governments of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger

conflicts.stakes: Gold (Mali and Burkina Faso are big producers), uranium (Niger), and the limits of Russia's reach in Africa.
conflicts.what: A jihadist insurgency across Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, whose military governments expelled French troops and turned to Russia.

card.blocNote: A US security partner and weapons buyer, a BRICS member, and a big buyer of AI chips. It struck Iran in 2026 after Iranian missiles hit US bases on its soil.
card.exposed: Iranian missiles, Hormuz, and US pressure over Dubai's role as a way around sanctions.
holds: Oil capacity built toward 5 million barrels a day, which is why it left OPEC
Dubai: the region's finance centre and the world's busiest international airport
Sovereign funds of well over a trillion dollars
A pipeline to Fujairah that skips Hormuz
card.leverage: Sovereign money, oil it can now pump without a quota, and a neutral market where Russian, Iranian, Western and Chinese money all meet.
card.name: United Arab Emirates
card.nameTh: สหรัฐอาหรับเอมิเรตส์
card.role: The Gulf's hub for trade and money, and since 1 May 2026 an oil producer free of OPEC quotas.
sells: Re-exports through Dubai: gold, phones, cars
card.thailand: Dubai is a key gold and transit hub for Thai trade. Gulf tourists and investors come too.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.note: Under Milei, the US's closest partner in South America, backed by a US Treasury currency swap in 2025.

card.blocNote: US treaty ally and a member of the Quad and AUKUS (nuclear submarines), even though most of its ore goes to China.
card.exposed: China buys about a third of its exports and banned several of them in 2020–22. It imports nearly all its fuel.
holds: About half of world lithium mining
Iron ore, and the largest rare-earth processor outside China (Lynas)
Uranium
card.leverage: Critical minerals outside China, which makes it the West's alternative rare-earth supply, plus LNG for Japan and Korea.
card.name: Australia
card.nameTh: ออสเตรเลีย
card.role: Asia's quarry: the largest exporter of iron ore and lithium, a top LNG and coal supplier, and closely allied with the US.
card.thailand: Free-trade partner since 2005: Thai pickups and cars go there, and Australia sells Thailand coal, gold and food.

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.note: Russia's closest ally; hosts Russian tactical nuclear weapons.

card.blocNote: A founding BRICS member and close to China, but a democracy that refuses to pick a side. It clashed with Washington over steep tariffs in 2025.
card.exposed: Depends on imported fertiliser and on commodity prices, and has recurring worries about its public finances.
holds: Farmland and water on a continental scale
Iron ore, niobium and rare-earth deposits
The Amazon
card.leverage: Food. It replaced the US as China's main soybean source during the trade wars.
card.name: Brazil
card.role: Latin America's giant: an agricultural superpower that feeds China, and a voice of the Global South.
sells: Crude oil from its deep offshore fields
card.thailand: Competes with Thailand in sugar and chicken exports, and supplies the soy in Thai animal feed.

card.blocNote: A founding NATO and G7 member, though relations with Washington soured over tariffs and annexation talk in 2025.
card.exposed: About three-quarters of its exports go to the US.
holds: The third-largest oil reserves (the oil sands)
Potash for the world's fertiliser
Uranium, critical minerals and fresh water
card.leverage: Energy and minerals the US cannot easily replace.
card.name: Canada
card.role: A resource superpower on America's border: the largest foreign supplier of US oil, gas, electricity and uranium.
sells: Crude oil, mostly to the US
card.thailand: Small but growing: food, potash fertiliser, and Canadian pension funds investing in Asia.

card.blocNote: Anchors the other side but prefers partners to allies. It keeps Russia's economy running and sent Iran dual-use parts and intelligence in the 2026 war, without fighting itself.
buys: Crude oil. It is the largest importer: Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and discounted Iranian crude
card.exposed: Imports about 70% of its oil, mostly by sea through Malacca (and, until March 2026, through Hormuz). It cannot yet make leading-edge chips, and it leans on exports while the property slump drags on demand at home.
holds: About two-thirds of rare-earth mining and about 90% of refining and magnet making
Most of the refining of lithium, cobalt and graphite for batteries
About 30% of the world's manufacturing output
About $3 trillion of foreign-exchange reserves
card.leverage: Export controls on rare earths, magnets, gallium and germanium. It used them in 2025 to force the Busan truce, and they are the sticking point at this week's Trump–Xi summit in Washington, Xi's first state visit in eleven years. It is also the largest customer of most commodity exporters.
card.name: China
card.role: The challenger superpower: the world's factory, its largest trading nation, and the only economy big enough to rival the US.
sells: EVs, batteries and solar panels, all at dominant world share
Steel, chemicals and processed critical minerals
card.thailand: Thailand's largest trading partner overall and biggest source of imports. It is the largest investor in new Thai factories (EVs, electronics), a major source of tourists, and at the end of the rail line through Laos.

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.note: A Russian and Chinese partner 150 km from Florida. Lost its Venezuelan oil lifeline after January 2026.

card.blocNote: A core NATO and EU member, rearming since 2025 with defence spending exempted from its debt brake.
buys: Energy: LNG, Norwegian pipeline gas, oil
card.exposed: Its car industry is losing ground to Chinese EVs, including inside China. It also faces high energy costs and US tariffs on its exports.
holds: World-class machine tools and industrial engineering
Europe's largest chemicals base
The anchor of the euro and the largest share of the EU budget
card.leverage: It sets Europe's line on China trade, on Ukraine aid and on fiscal rules, and it is the EU's largest funder.
card.name: Germany
card.role: Europe's largest economy and industrial core: an export machine that lost its cheap Russian gas.
card.thailand: Thailand's largest EU trading partner. German firms assemble cars and source parts there, and EU–Thailand free-trade talks have been running since 2023.

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.note: Sovereign over Greenland. Signed the 18 Sep 2026 security deal that gives the US two more bases there, after twenty months of pressure from Washington.

card.blocNote: Takes US military aid and joined BRICS in 2024; buys arms from every side.
buys: Fuel and gas, including from Israel
card.exposed: Houthi attacks have cut Suez traffic sharply since 2024. It also faces debt and currency crises and a large food import bill.
holds: The Suez Canal, about a tenth of world trade in normal times
The Sinai border with Gaza
card.leverage: Suez, and the crossing into Gaza.
card.name: Egypt
card.role: Keeper of the Suez Canal, the most populous Arab state, and the world's largest wheat importer.
sells: LNG, when it has gas to spare
card.thailand: Buys Thai rice. Thai cargo to Europe goes through Suez, or the long way around Africa when the Red Sea is unsafe.

card.blocNote: A founding NATO and EU member, and the loudest advocate of Europe standing on its own. It has offered to discuss extending its nuclear umbrella to European allies.
card.exposed: Public debt around 115% of GDP and political gridlock. Its bond spread over Germany widens every time a government falls.
holds: Nuclear power for about two-thirds of its electricity, and the fuel industry behind it
Nuclear weapons and a UN veto
Pacific and Indian Ocean territories (New Caledonia's nickel)
Europe's largest arms export industry
card.leverage: Arms sales (Rafales to India, Indonesia and the Gulf), nuclear know-how, its UN veto, and weight in EU decisions.
card.name: France
card.role: The EU's only nuclear power, with a UN veto and territories across three oceans.
card.thailand: Aircraft (much of Thai Airways' fleet is Airbus), tourism, and luxury spending.

card.blocNote: America's closest intelligence partner (Five Eyes), an AUKUS member, and one of Ukraine's largest backers in Europe.
card.exposed: Imports much of its food and energy, and growth is weak. Its bond market punishes fiscal surprises, as in 2022.
holds: The City of London: the largest FX market and the global gold market
A nuclear deterrent and a UN veto
North Sea oil and gas, now in decline
card.leverage: Finance and insurance. Shipping is insured in London, which makes it where sanctions and oil price caps get enforced.
card.name: United Kingdom
card.nameTh: สหราชอาณาจักร
card.role: A financial and nuclear power: London is the world's largest currency market and its gold vault, and Britain holds a UN veto.
card.thailand: A big source of long-stay tourists and investment. London's gold price is the one Thai gold shops follow.

card.blocNote: Under Danish sovereignty and NATO cover. The 18 September 2026 US–Denmark–Greenland deal gives the US two new bases and permanent military access, with Russia and China locked out.
card.exposed: Depends on Danish grants for about half of public spending, and is a tiny population facing great powers.
holds: Rare-earth and critical-mineral deposits
Pituffik Space Base, part of US missile warning
The Arctic approaches and new polar shipping lanes
card.leverage: It sits under the shortest missile path between Russia and the US, and holds minerals outside China's control.
card.name: Greenland
card.role: An Arctic island of about 57,000 people, self-governing within Denmark, that the US has pushed to control since 2025.
sells: Fish and shrimp, nearly all of its exports
card.thailand: No direct link. It reaches Thailand only through rare-earth prices.

card.blocNote: Joined BRICS in 2025 yet trains with the US military. The heart of 'free and active' non-alignment.
card.exposed: Heavy dependence on Chinese investment and demand, and a weak rupiah.
holds: About half of world nickel output
Coal
The shores of the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits
card.leverage: It banned raw-ore exports to force processing at home, and now sets the nickel price.
card.name: Indonesia
card.nameTh: อินโดนีเซีย
card.role: The fourth most populous country, Southeast Asia's largest economy, and the nickel supplier of the EV era.
sells: Nickel and stainless steel, processed at home in Chinese-built smelters
card.thailand: Thailand's ASEAN rival for car and EV investment, and a large market for Thai cars, sugar and machinery.

card.blocNote: Sits in the Quad with the US and in BRICS and the SCO with China and Russia. It buys Russian oil and arms and assembles iPhones for America. On principle, it signs up with neither side.
buys: Crude oil (about 85% imported; Russia has been the largest supplier since 2022)
Gold. It is one of the two largest buyers
card.exposed: Oil imports (Hormuz), disputed borders with China and Pakistan (India and Pakistan fought in May 2025), and US pressure over Russian oil: a February 2026 deal cut US tariffs in exchange for ending those purchases, which India has not fully done, and a new US law allows tariffs of up to 100% on Russian-oil buyers.
holds: The largest working-age population on earth
A deep engineering and IT workforce
Pharmaceutical manufacturing scale
Nuclear weapons and the Indian Ocean's largest navy
card.leverage: Its size makes it the partner both sides court. It is the only 'China plus one' manufacturing alternative at real scale, and its gold and oil buying moves prices.
card.name: India
card.role: The most populous country and the fastest-growing large economy: the swing state that matters most.
sells: Refined fuels, much of it refined from Russian crude
Generic pharmaceuticals, as the world's main supplier
card.thailand: A fast-growing market and a top source of tourists. Also Thailand's rival in rice exports.

card.blocNote: Russia gave it intelligence and China sent dual-use parts in 2026, but neither has fought for it. The Supreme Leader was killed in the opening strikes, and the regime has held on.
card.exposed: A US naval blockade of its ports since 13 April 2026, strikes on its infrastructure, sanctions, and a collapsing currency. A Pakistan-brokered ceasefire in April broke down in early July when it attacked ships in Hormuz.
holds: The north shore of the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of world oil before the war
Huge oil and gas reserves, including South Pars
Missiles and drones, and allied forces in Iraq, Yemen and Lebanon
card.leverage: Hormuz. Closing it has kept Brent close to or above $100 for most of the war, in what the IEA calls the largest oil supply disruption in history.
card.name: Iran
card.role: The Shia power of the Gulf, at war with the US and Israel since 28 February 2026, and holding the Strait of Hormuz hostage.
sells: Crude oil, mostly to China at a discount and around sanctions
card.thailand: Little direct trade, but its war is Thailand's biggest energy-cost shock since 2022, because Thailand imports most of its crude from the Gulf.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.note: Home to Iranian-backed militias. Its oil exits through Hormuz, and Saudi aircraft struck militias on its soil during the 2026 war.

card.blocNote: America's closest partner in the region. It opened the war on Iran with the US on 28 February 2026.
card.exposed: Missile and drone attacks from Iran and its allies, the cost of a long war, and diplomatic isolation over Gaza.
holds: A deep tech and cyber sector
Missile defence (Iron Dome, Arrow)
Offshore gas exported to Egypt and Jordan
card.leverage: Military reach across the region and influence in Washington.
card.name: Israel
card.role: The Middle East's military and tech power, an undeclared nuclear state, and at war on several fronts since October 2023.
card.thailand: Tens of thousands of Thai farm workers live there. Thais were among the victims and hostages of 7 October 2023.

card.blocNote: Treaty ally of the US since 1951, and rearming toward 2% of GDP as China and North Korea build up.
buys: LNG, crude and coal. Nearly 90% of its energy is imported
card.exposed: Almost all its energy is imported, much of it through Hormuz and Malacca. China has squeezed it since November 2025 (seafood ban, fewer flights, a ban on dual-use exports to its military) over the prime minister's Taiwan remarks. It also faces a shrinking population and public debt above 200% of GDP.
holds: Materials in the chip chain nobody else makes at scale: photoresists, wafers, specialty gases
The world's largest net foreign assets, and the biggest foreign holding of US Treasuries
Advanced manufacturing and robotics
card.leverage: Its money. Japanese savers and institutions own trillions of dollars of foreign bonds; when yen rates rise and that money comes home, bond markets everywhere feel it.
card.name: Japan
card.role: The fourth-largest economy and America's anchor ally in Asia, hosting the largest US troop presence abroad.
sells: Chip-making equipment and materials (Tokyo Electron, photoresists, silicon wafers)
card.thailand: Thailand's largest foreign investor for decades. Most Thai car plants are Japanese (Toyota, Isuzu, Honda), and the eastern seaboard was built around them.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.note: Sends its oil to Europe through a Russian port (CPC). Sells uranium to all sides.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.note: China's closest partner in ASEAN (the Chinese-funded Ream naval base). Fought Thailand along the border in July and again in December 2025; a ceasefire has held through 2026, but relations are still tense after Thailand cancelled the MOU 44 maritime agreement.

card.blocNote: US treaty ally with about 28,000 US troops. China punished it economically in 2017 for hosting a US missile-defence system.
buys: Crude oil and LNG, mostly from the Middle East
card.exposed: Energy through Hormuz, China as its largest market, North Korea, and US tariffs on its cars.
holds: HBM memory, the bottleneck part in every AI accelerator
The world's leading shipyards
A large nuclear power industry

events.author: night desk
events.drive: Kim Jong Un has refused any renewed talks with Seoul or a phased nuclear deal, even as South Korea's President Lee pressed the UN this week for the US to resume negotiations. Testing an upgraded hypersonic glide vehicle, one that manoeuvres in flight and is harder for missile defences to track, is Pyongyang's way of showing it keeps building serious military technology regardless of diplomacy. It also has an export angle: North Korea supplies Russia with shells, missiles and troops for the Ukraine war under their 2024 defence pact, and a working hypersonic system adds to what it has to sell or share. Kim rejected any phased deal the same weekend, and Lee's appeal at the UN on 23 September came three days after the test: Pyongyang is showing leverage, not looking for an opening.
events.headline: North Korea test-fired a new hypersonic glide missile off its east coast on 20 September, its most advanced weapon test yet.

losers.why: Faces a more capable, harder-to-shoot-down threat on its border, undercutting President Lee's push for talks.
The missile flew off North Korea's east coast, inside the range that already worries Japanese air-defence planners.

macro.why: A more advanced North Korean missile adds a small risk discount to Korean equities.
Adds a sliver to the general geopolitical risk premium markets price in.

sources.title: North Korea test-fires apparent HGV-equipped Hwaseongpho-11 variant
North Korea Tests New Hypersonic Missile
North Korea Tests New Hwasong-11Ma Hypersonic Missile

events.thb: Little direct effect on a baht portfolio. North Korea trades almost nothing with Thailand; the channel here is indirect, through Korean and Japanese investors and tourists who grow more cautious if the peninsula gets tenser.
events.title: North Korea test-fires a new hypersonic-glide missile
events.titleTh: เกาหลีเหนือทดสอบขีปนาวุธร่อนความเร็วเหนือเสียงรุ่นใหม่
events.usd: Markets barely moved; a single North Korean test rarely does. It nudges the regional risk premium sitting under Korean and Japanese assets, including the chipmakers and carmakers many US-listed funds hold for Asia exposure, but it takes a pattern of tests or a real crisis, not one launch, to move the dollar book.
events.watch: Whether Kim agrees to meet Trump, another test of the same missile, and South Korea's next move after Lee's UN appeal for talks.

winners.why: Demonstrates a harder-to-intercept missile, adding leverage in any future talks and something to offer Russia under their defence pact.
A working North Korean hypersonic system is a potential technology transfer for a country at war and short of advanced missiles.

events.author: session
events.drive: Greenland sits under the shortest route for missiles and bombers between Russia and North America, beside new Arctic shipping lanes, and on rare-earth deposits outside China's control. From January 2025 President Trump pressed to buy or take the island, straining relations with Denmark and NATO. The deal signed on 18 September gives Washington what it mainly wanted, military access and a say over who else gets in, without the transfer of sovereignty that Denmark and Greenlanders refused.
events.headline: After twenty months of pressure to take Greenland, Washington settled for more bases and a veto over Chinese and Russian investment, while Denmark keeps sovereignty.

losers.why: Shut out of bases and of sensitive investment such as mining, closing one of its routes into Arctic resources and shipping.
Faces more US radar and missile warning on its northern flank.
The right to self-determination is written in, but big decisions about land and minerals now run through a security deal Greenland did not write alone.

sources.title: U.S. and Denmark reach deal to build U.S. military presence in Greenland
What's in the Greenland agreement between U.S. and Denmark
Greenland deal: What did the US and Denmark actually agree to?
Trump says US has 'permanent control' of Greenland security: Does it?

events.thb: Almost no direct effect on Thailand or the baht. It reaches a Thai investor only through rare-earth prices, and as a sign of how Washington now treats allies: pressure first, then a deal on its terms.
events.title: US, Denmark and Greenland sign a security deal
events.titleTh: สหรัฐฯ เดนมาร์ก และกรีนแลนด์ลงนามข้อตกลงความมั่นคง
events.usd: Little effect on broad markets; the crisis had already faded from prices. It gives modest support to Western rare-earth and critical-mineral companies, and removes one source of US–Europe friction while the Iran war and the China truce matter far more.
events.watch: Where the two new bases go and when building starts; whether any Greenland mining project gets US backing; Greenland's own politics, where independence parties may push back; and NATO's Arctic plans.

winners.why: More bases, and more radar and missile warning at Pituffik, plus the power to keep out rival bases and 'sensitive' investment, reportedly including minerals, without buying or governing the island.
Keeps sovereignty and ends a twenty-month crisis with its closest ally that had strained NATO.
Greenland's deposits become a more investable Western source, and Washington has signalled it wants them developed by friendly hands.

events.author: session
events.drive: With Hormuz throttled since March, Saudi Arabia had been sending oil west through its East–West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, the Gulf's main way around the strait. Iran's strategy in the war is to raise the price of oil and gas until Washington gives way, and its allies have now gone after that second exit. Drones launched from Iraq damaged the pipeline, and the Houthis' advance puts them astride the strait Yanbu's tankers must pass to reach Asia.
events.headline: Iran-backed Houthis took control of Yemen's Red Sea coast and an island in the Bab el-Mandeb, as drones knocked out the Saudi pipeline that carried oil around Hormuz.

losers.why: No crude has left Yanbu since 11 September and the pipeline will be out for weeks, cutting its main route around Hormuz; Aramco has cancelled cargoes to Europe.
Suez income, already down since 2024, falls further.
Thailand buys most of its crude from the Gulf, and its cargo to Europe already detours around Africa.
China, Japan, Korea and India buy most of the Gulf's oil, and both of its exits are now under threat.

macro.why: Both of the Gulf's export routes are under attack at the same time.
A bigger oil import bill weakens the baht against the dollar.
Higher energy prices lift the inflation the bond market expects.

sources.title: Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize a strategic port and island, opening a new battlefront
Houthis control key shipping route after gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast
Yemen's Houthis capture a Red Sea island in threat to shipping
Oil prices rise 3% after strikes on crucial Saudi pipeline, repairs to take weeks
Saudi Aramco Cancels European Crude Cargoes as Key Pipeline Stays Shut

events.thb: Bad for Thailand. A bigger oil import bill widens the trade deficit and weighs on the baht, while fuel and electricity push Thai inflation up. Exports to Europe face longer, costlier voyages.
events.title: Houthis seize Yemen's Red Sea coast and Mayun island
events.titleTh: กลุ่มฮูตียึดชายฝั่งทะเลแดงของเยเมนและเกาะมายูน
events.usd: Oil rose about 3% on the pipeline strikes and forecasts for the rest of 2026 were raised. Dearer oil lifts inflation risk, which argues against quick Fed cuts and weighs on long-duration tech; energy producers and tanker owners gain.
events.watch: Whether tankers load at Yanbu again and when the pipeline is repaired; any US or Saudi move to retake the coast or Mayun; attacks on ships in the Bab el-Mandeb; and the US–Iran talks in New York.

winners.why: Leverage over both of the Gulf's exits at once, the pressure it wants before any deal with Washington.
Every extra dollar on oil is revenue for Moscow's war budget, and Russian tankers have mostly been spared by the Houthis.
Higher prices, and Asian and European buyers hunting for supply away from the Gulf.
Longer routes and higher risk push freight and insurance rates up.

ASEAN.label: ASEAN
ASEAN.what: Southeast Asia's eleven, Thailand included: a trade bloc that decides by consensus, which makes it slow and hard to split.

AUKUS.label: AUKUS
AUKUS.what: Australia, the UK and the US: nuclear-powered submarines for Australia, plus shared military technology.

BRICS.label: BRICS
BRICS.what: The emerging-economy club, expanded since 2024. It holds very different countries together, united mostly by wanting a world less run by the dollar. Partner countries attend without full membership.

EU.label: EU
EU.what: The single market of 27 states: one trade policy, one sanctions list, and the euro for twenty of them.

G7.label: G7
G7.what: The rich democracies' club, where sanctions and price caps get agreed. The EU also sits at the table.

NATO.label: NATO
NATO.what: The US-led military alliance. An attack on one is an attack on all (Article 5).

OPEC+.label: OPEC+
OPEC+.what: The oil producers who set output quotas together, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia. The UAE left on 1 May 2026. Members are OPEC; partners are the non-OPEC producers who joined the quotas.

Quad.label: Quad
Quad.what: US, Japan, India and Australia: a security dialogue aimed at balancing China at sea. Not a treaty.

SCO.label: SCO
SCO.what: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation: the China- and Russia-led Eurasian security forum. India and Pakistan both sit in it.

USPAC.label: US Asia allies
USPAC.what: America's treaty allies in Asia and the Pacific, each bound by its own defence treaty with the US. Thailand is one of them, and so is its hedging.

pieces.bishop: A regional power, or one that holds something the rest cannot do without.
pieces.king: A superpower. The board is arranged around these two.
pieces.pawn: Small on the board, but at the centre of something that moves it.
pieces.queen: A great power with reach beyond its own region.
pieces.rook: A heavyweight economy or energy power that shapes its region.

relationTypes.ally: A formal defence commitment: a treaty or pact.
relationTypes.partner: Close cooperation without a defence commitment.
relationTypes.pressure: One squeezing the other: sanctions, export controls, bans. Runs from the first to the second.
relationTypes.rival: Strategic competition: they plan against each other.

NATO. Germany hosts the main US bases and logistics hub in Europe, including Ramstein.
NATO. US troops rotate through Poland, the alliance's eastern front and the hub for aid to Ukraine.

Warmer since 2025. Pakistan's army chief brokered the April 2026 US–Iran ceasefire and hosted the talks in Islamabad.
Weapons (now mostly paid for by European allies), intelligence, and a 2025 minerals deal. Washington is also the main mediator with Moscow.

USMCA partners and each other's largest trading partner. Strained by tariffs, migration and US threats against cartels; the USMCA review is due in 2026.
Close to an alliance: a 2022 security declaration and a reciprocal-access deal that lets their forces train in each other's territory.
A 2024 reciprocal-access agreement, and joint drills with the US after the July 2026 clashes at Scarborough.

The Union State and the CSTO. Russian tactical nuclear weapons are stationed in Belarus.

'Iron brothers'. Most of Pakistan's weapons are Chinese, and the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor runs to the port of Gwadar.

A mutual-defence pact signed in September 2025, putting nuclear-armed Pakistan's military behind Saudi Arabia.
The 2021 Shusha Declaration, a mutual-defence commitment between the two Turkic states.
The rivalry that shapes the board: tariffs, chip controls and rare-earth controls, paused by the Busan truce until 10 November. Xi is in Washington this week, his first state visit in eleven years.
Nuclear rivals. The US sanctions Russian oil and banks while also mediating in Ukraine.
No diplomatic ties since the Korean War. Seoul is pushing for Trump–Kim talks; Kim rejects any phased deal.
Rivals since the deadly 2020 Galwan border clash. A 2024 border deal and Modi's 2025 visit to China have eased tensions.
In a deep freeze since November 2025, when Japan's prime minister said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could draw Japan in.
Beijing claims Taiwan and rehearses blockades; its coast guard now patrols east of the island.
Coast-guard clashes at Scarborough and Second Thomas shoals: three in one week in July 2026.
Two ruling communist parties with deep trade ties, but rival claims to the Paracel and Spratly islands.
Four wars and a nuclear standoff over Kashmir; the latest fighting was in May 2025.
Rivals for the Gulf. A China-brokered détente (2023) ended in 2026, when Iran struck Saudi oil sites and Saudi Arabia struck back.
Sanctions on Russia's oil majors and banks, and a new law allowing tariffs of up to 100% on countries that keep buying Russian oil.
Maximum-pressure sanctions, and since 13 April 2026 a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Export controls on advanced AI chips and chip-making tools, partly eased under the truce.

Since November 2025: a seafood ban, fewer flights, warnings against travel, and from January 2026 a ban on dual-use exports to Japanese military users.
The embargo in place since 1962. Cuba also lost its Venezuelan oil in 2026.
China buys most of Brazil's soybeans and iron ore; both are founding BRICS members.
Turkey buys Russian gas and oil, and Russia's Rosatom is building its first nuclear plant, while Turkey sits in NATO.

A 2022 free-trade deal. The UAE is a hub for India's oil, gold and diaspora money.

chokeStatus.disrupted: Closed or under attack; traffic a fraction of normal.
chokeStatus.reduced: Open, with traffic well below normal.

chokepoints.bypass: Saudi Arabia's East–West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea (up to about 7 mb/d, but damaged by drones in September and out for weeks) and the UAE's pipeline to Fujairah (about 1.5 mb/d). Qatar's LNG has no way around.
chokepoints.carries: About 21 million barrels a day of oil in 2025, a fifth of world use, and about a fifth of the world's LNG. Most of its crude goes to Asia.
chokepoints.name: Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints.nameTh: ช่องแคบฮอร์มุซ
chokepoints.now: Iran closed it in March 2026. US-escorted convoys have brought oil back to about half its normal flow, but LNG tankers barely moved for six months; Qatar's first cargoes are only trickling back in September.
chokepoints.thailand: Most of Thailand's crude comes through it, and so does its rice to Iraq, Thailand's second-largest rice buyer.

chokepoints.bypass: Around the Cape of Good Hope, adding 10 to 14 days between Asia and Europe.
chokepoints.carries: About 4 million barrels a day of oil in 2025, half its level before the Houthi attacks, and the southern gate to the Suez Canal.
chokepoints.name: Bab el-Mandeb
chokepoints.nameTh: ช่องแคบบับเอลมันเดบ
chokepoints.now: In September 2026 the Houthis took Yemen's whole Red Sea coast and Mayun island in the strait itself.
chokepoints.thailand: Thai exports to Europe used to go this way; most now go around Africa.

chokepoints.bypass: Around the Cape of Good Hope.
chokepoints.carries: About 5 million barrels a day of oil with the SUMED pipeline in 2025, down from about 9 before 2024, and roughly a tenth of world trade in normal times.
chokepoints.name: Suez Canal
chokepoints.now: Traffic has not recovered since the Houthi attacks began in late 2023. Most container lines still sail around Africa, and Egypt has lost much of its canal income.
chokepoints.thailand: The short route for Thai exports to Europe.

chokepoints.bypass: The Sunda and Lombok straits through Indonesia, a few days longer. Thailand's proposed Kra land bridge would cut across its own isthmus instead.
chokepoints.carries: About 24 million barrels a day of oil, the most of any strait, and most of East Asia's trade with the Gulf, Africa and Europe.
chokepoints.name: Strait of Malacca
chokepoints.nameTh: ช่องแคบมะละกา
chokepoints.now: Open. Every Gulf cargo bound for China, Japan, Korea or Thailand still has to pass it.
chokepoints.thailand: Everything Thailand buys from the Gulf and sells west of Singapore passes it.

chokepoints.bypass: East of Taiwan through the Philippine Sea, a day or two longer, unless a blockade closes both.
chokepoints.carries: The main lane between Northeast Asia and everywhere west of it; almost half the world's container ships passed through it in 2022.
chokepoints.name: Taiwan Strait
chokepoints.nameTh: ช่องแคบไต้หวัน
chokepoints.now: Open, but Chinese coast-guard patrols and blockade drills make it the strait markets watch for a sudden stop.
chokepoints.thailand: Thai trade with Japan, Korea and northern China.

chokepoints.bypass: None by sea: it is the only way out of the Black Sea.
chokepoints.carries: About 3 to 4 million barrels a day of Russian and Kazakh oil, and most of the grain from Russia and Ukraine.
chokepoints.name: Turkish Straits
chokepoints.nameTh: ช่องแคบบอสพอรัส
chokepoints.now: Open to merchant ships. Turkey has kept warships out since 2022 under the Montreux Convention, and drone strikes on Black Sea ports and tankers keep insurance costs high.
chokepoints.thailand: Sets world wheat and fertiliser prices.

chokepoints.bypass: Around Cape Horn, or across the US by rail.
chokepoints.carries: About 5% of world seaborne trade, including US grain and LNG bound for Asia.
chokepoints.name: Panama Canal
chokepoints.nameTh: คลองปานามา
chokepoints.now: Open, with water levels back to normal after the 2023–24 drought. Washington pressed Panama in 2025 over Chinese influence around the canal.
chokepoints.thailand: Little direct trade, but it sets the cost of US grain and LNG in Asia.

chokepoints.carries: The long way around Africa: about 6 million barrels a day of oil in 2025 and most Asia–Europe container traffic since 2024.
chokepoints.name: Cape of Good Hope
chokepoints.nameTh: แหลมกู๊ดโฮป
chokepoints.now: Busier than before 2024, carrying the traffic the Red Sea lost.
chokepoints.thailand: Thai cargo to Europe now takes this route; longer voyages mean higher freight costs.
